cards.lead: Microwave oven cooking in the United States
cards.name: Microwave oven cooking, Raytheon and the Radarange
cards.summary: Raytheon's Radarange, marketed in 1947 as the first commercial microwave oven, began cooking with microwave energy in the United States.
cards.description: Percy Spencer and Raytheon worked to develop a microwave oven for cooking and filed a patent on 8 October 1945. The first commercial model, the Radarange, was marketed in 1947; it cost $3,000, weighed about 750 pounds and stood six feet tall, and home-use models took about twenty years more.
cards.origin_note: The sources call the Radarange the first commercial microwave oven and name no earlier one, so first known is the reading they support.

impact.note: Scores kept from the lead; the sources fetched give no household or country figures, so reach is not revised.

events.label: 8 October 1945
events.statement: Spencer and Raytheon filed a patent application for a microwave oven to be used for cooking on 8 October 1945.
events.quote: filed for a patent on October 8, 1945

events.statement: The first commercial microwave oven, the Radarange, was marketed in 1947.
events.quote: The first commercial microwave oven was called “Radarange,” marketed in 1947.

open_questions: The lead's Waltham, Massachusetts location, the 1967 countertop model and household ownership by country are not in the sources fetched.
EBSCO says Raytheon patented the oven in 1945, while Lemelson gives the grant as 24 January 1950; a primary patent record would settle the grant date.

cards.lead: Seed-crop farming in eastern North America
cards.note: The source dates the domestication to about 5,000 years ago (about 3050 BCE), not the lead's range c. 3000-1800 BCE, and does not address whether it was independent, so origin is set to unknown.
cards.name: Seed-crop farming, eastern North America
cards.summary: People in eastern North America domesticated squash, sunflower, marshelder and pitseed goosefoot about 5,000 years ago, the first plant domestication on the continent.
cards.description: A 2016 University of Utah study of radiocarbon-dated sites in eastern North America concludes that a population boom and scarce wild food led people there to domesticate wild food plants for the first time on the continent, about 5,000 years ago. The release names squash, sunflower, marshelder and pitseed goosefoot as the plants involved.
cards.origin_note: The fetched sources describe the domestication as occurring in eastern North America but do not say whether it was independent of Mesoamerican crops.

impact.note: Depth 2 kept: the study says domestication allowed large numbers of people to live in one place; reach and generativity kept from the lead, and sunflower's later use as an oil crop is not in the fetched sources.

cards.why: The 2016 study argues that a population boom between about 6,900 and 5,200 years ago, and the resulting scarcity of wild foods, prompted domestication.

events.label: about 5,000 years ago
events.statement: Radiocarbon-dated archaeological evidence from eastern North America is taken to show plant domestication there about 5,000 years ago.
events.quote: concluded that a population boom and scarce food explain why people in eastern North America domesticated plants for the first time on the continent about 5,000 years ago

sources.title: Population boom preceded early farming (University of Utah news release)

open_questions: The 2016 study in Royal Society Open Science was not opened; the site dates for Phillips Spring, Hayes, Napoleon Hollow and Riverton, and the lead's c. 1800 BCE end date, need the paper or site reports.
Independence from Mesoamerican crops and the date when these crops were abandoned are not in the fetched sources.

cards.note: The earliest dated record is a shipment from Gran Canaria to Antwerp on 28 November 1567, earlier than the lead's c. 1570. The fetched source does not support long-day adaptation or the field-staple dates of c. 1700-1800, so the card covers arrival only.
cards.name: Potato introduction to Europe
cards.summary: Potatoes reached Europe through the Canary Islands, with a documented shipment from Gran Canaria to Antwerp in November 1567.
cards.description: Potatoes brought from the Andes reached Europe through the Canary Islands, which served as the hub for distributing the plant. A document in the archives of Las Palmas records potatoes shipped from Gran Canaria to Antwerp on 28 November 1567. The sources fetched do not describe how the crop was later adapted to northern European day lengths.
cards.origin_note: The record shows the crop distributed from the Canary Islands, an evidenced transmission from the Andes rather than an independent achievement.

impact.note: Scores kept from the lead; the fetched source gives no population figures, so the effect on population is not checked.

events.label: 28 November 1567
events.statement: Potatoes shipped from Gran Canaria to Antwerp on 28 November 1567 are recorded in a document from the archives of Las Palmas.
events.quote: a document from the archives of Las Palmas which mentions a few dishes of potatoes that were shipped from Gran Canaria to Antwerp on 28 November 1567

sources.title: The victory march of the potato across Europe began in the Low Countries

open_questions: The long-day adaptation of European varieties, and how and when it arose, need a plant-genetics source.

cards.lead: Transgenic crop plants in Belgium and the United States
cards.note: The 1983 papers report chimeric genes expressed in plant cells, not whole transgenic plants, and the sources do not settle which group was first, so origin is set to unknown.
cards.name: Transgenic plant cells, Ghent, Cambridge and St. Louis
cards.summary: In 1983 Ghent, Cambridge and St. Louis groups reported bacterial antibiotic-resistance genes working in plant cells, the basis of later transgenic crops.
cards.description: Herrera-Estrella and colleagues at Ghent expressed a chimeric kanamycin-resistance gene in tobacco cells carried by the Ti plasmid, published in 1983. Bevan, Flavell and Chilton, at Cambridge and Washington University in St. Louis, built a chimaeric antibiotic-resistance gene that conferred G418 resistance on transformed plant cells, published in Nature on 14 July 1983.
cards.origin_note: Two groups reported closely related results in 1983 and the fetched sources do not establish which was first.

impact.note: Scores kept from the lead; the sources fetched do not show the crop area reached, so reach is not checked.

events.statement: Herrera-Estrella and colleagues showed that a chimeric kanamycin-resistance gene, carried into tobacco cells by the Ti plasmid, was expressed in plant cells.
events.quote: The chimeric NOS-APH(3')II gene, when transferred to tobacco cells using the Ti plasmid as a gene vector, was expressed and conferred resistance to kanamycin to the plant cells.

events.label: 14 July 1983
events.statement: Bevan, Flavell and Chilton reported a chimaeric antibiotic-resistance gene that confers G418 resistance on transformed plant cells, published in Nature.
events.quote: We have exploited the regulatory elements of this gene to construct a chimaeric gene that confers antibiotic resistance on transformed plant cells.

sources.title: Chimeric genes as dominant selectable markers in plant cells
A chimaeric antibiotic resistance gene as a selectable marker for plant cell transformation

The commercial release dates (1994-1996) and the share of world cropland are not sourced in the fetched text.
Whole transgenic plant regeneration from these cell systems needs a source.

cards.lead: Pure yeast culture brewing in Copenhagen
cards.note: The 1883 date and Carlsberg setting are confirmed, but Hansen took up pure-culture methods developed by Pasteur and Koch, so the origin is derived rather than first known.
cards.name: Pure yeast culture brewing, Carlsberg
cards.summary: Emil Christian Hansen's single-cell yeast cultures, first brewed at Carlsberg on 12 November 1883, gave brewers a yeast free of wild types.
cards.description: At the Carlsberg brewery in Copenhagen, Emil Christian Hansen grew yeast cultures from a single cell, because wild yeast types had spoiled the brewing yeast. The first brew with the pure culture was made on 12 November 1883, and Jacobsen refused to patent the method, so it spread across the world.
cards.origin_note: Hansen applied pure-culture methods that Pasteur and Koch had developed, so the method was transmitted before it was used for brewing.

impact.note: Scores kept from the lead; the fetched source supports the spread of the method but not the claim that it set the method for industrial microbiology.

cards.why: Wild yeast types mixed into the brewing yeast had spoiled the beer, which the pure cultures were meant to prevent.

events.label: 12 November 1883
events.statement: The Carlsberg brewery made its first brew with Hansen's pure yeast culture on 12 November 1883.
events.quote: 12 November 1883 became a red-letter day in the history of brewing

open_questions: The coordinates are from general knowledge of the Carlsberg site, not from the fetched text, and should be checked.
The fetched text does not give the year of the single-cell isolation, only that the cultures were developed; how quickly other breweries adopted the method is not sourced.
The text says Hansen's work followed Pasteur and Koch; the relation of the method to their work needs a history-of-science source.
